entries.name: Roman road (via / strata)
entries.era: 312 BCE to ~500 CE (roads reused into the Middle Ages)
entries.purpose: arterial military and trade route across the empire
layout: dead-straight segments between surveyed points, ignoring contour where possible
raised cambered core so rain runs off into side ditches
deep foundation layers (statumen, rudus, nucleus, summum dorsum)
milestone every Roman mile (1,480 m)
entries.found: on the flattest and straightest line between cities; plains, coasts and passes
entries.notes: Via Appia (312 BCE) opened the network; by its height the empire held ~400,000 km of roads, half of it paved.

entries.name: Stone arch bridge
entries.purpose: permanent span over rivers and gorges for foot, cart and pack traffic
layout: one to many arches; older Roman work favors semicircular, later work segmental (flatter, longer spans)
piers end in cutwaters to split the flood current
road deck cambered over the crowns
entries.found: at every settled river crossing that mattered; many Roman spans still carry traffic
entries.notes: Puente de Alcántara (Hispania, 106 CE) has carried carts for ~1,900 years. Arch stone in pure compression is the most durable span humans build.

entries.name: Iron/steel truss bridge
entries.purpose: cheap, strong railway and road spans of 30-80 m
layout: two parallel trusses either side of the deck, or a through-truss the deck passes inside
panel lengths 5-10 m between verticals
on rail lines usually track carried on timber stringers over the deck
entries.found: across every small river on 19th- and early 20th-century rail lines
entries.notes: The Pratt truss (1844) put diagonals in tension and was mass-produced with pinned joints, so remote crossings went up fast.

entries.name: Suspension bridge
materials: wrought-iron chains or parallel steel wire cables
entries.purpose: clear long spans (150 m to over 1 km) over broad water with no mid piers
parts: main cables draped between towers and anchored in massive blocks
layout: cables sag in a catenary; load is pulled out and down into the anchorages
towers carry clear vertical compression only
deck must be aerodynamically stiff — open trussed deck or streamlined box girder
entries.found: at broad river mouths, straits and bays where piers cannot be founded
entries.notes: Telford's Menai Strait bridge (Wales, 1826) proved iron chains; Tacoma Narrows (1940) proved the deck needs aerodynamic care. Modern spans exceed 2 km.

entries.name: Rope suspension footbridge
materials: twisted grass or ichu rope (now wire rope)
entries.purpose: lightweight crossing of gorges for foot and pack traffic
parts: stone anchor points on each cliff
layout: deck sags between anchor points; hand ropes lashed to deck every few planks
single file only; one person or one pack animal at a time
rope buds and anchors inspected and re-braided on a fixed cycle
entries.found: across Himalayan and Andean gorges where no pier can stand
entries.notes: Peru's Q'eswachaka bridge has been re-braided by the Quechua community for some 600 years, in an annual festival.

entries.name: Railway viaduct
entries.purpose: carry a level rail line across a valley too deep or wide to embank cheaply
layout: many equal spans; rise of each arch chosen so the soffit clears peak flood
curved in plan where the line sweeps a hillside (Glenfinnan)
track on ballast directly on the arch fill
entries.found: on mountain and branch lines crossing river gorges
entries.notes: Glenfinnan (Scotland, opened 1901) runs 21 mass-concrete arches, 380 m long and 30 m above the River Finnan — still in service.

entries.name: Timber railroad trestle
entries.purpose: race a rail line across a ravine before fill could be hauled in
layout: repeating bents every 3-6 m, like a giant sawhorse row
bracing triangulates every bent in both directions
meant as scaffolding for tomorrow's earthfill, not as a monument
entries.found: on 19th-century western US lines; most were buried under fill within a decade
entries.notes: Wyoming's Dale Creek trestle (1868) rose ~30 m; it survived barely 30 years before embankment replaced it.

entries.name: Railway station
entries.purpose: passenger and parcel interchange; the town-facing door of the railway
layout: track and platforms on axis, town forecourt in front
train shed spans all tracks with a single arched iron-and-glass roof
goods yard and sidings behind for freight
entries.found: every town the railway reached; termini reshaped city edges
entries.notes: Liverpool Road, Manchester (1830) is the world's oldest surviving intercity terminus; London's termini (St Pancras, 1868) made arrival a piece of theatre.

entries.name: Railway tunnel
materials: brick or stone lining (modern concrete segments)
entries.purpose: carry a rail line straight through a mountain instead of over it
layout: two headings driven from both faces to meet in the middle
gentle grade; clearance for the loading gauge at every section
refuge niches along tunnels too narrow for two lines
entries.found: through the great ranges that blocked rail expansion — Alps, Appalachians, Andes
entries.notes: The Mont Cenis tunnel (France-Italy, 1857-1871, 13.7 km) was hand-drilled from both portals over 14 years; it put the Alps behind a 3-hour train.

entries.name: Pound lock
entries.purpose: lift or drop a boat between two water levels without emptying the reach
layout: boat enters, gates shut behind it, paddles fill or drain the chamber ~3 m at a time
flights of locks stair-step a steep reach
single lock alternation saves water — each filling comes from the upper pound
entries.found: on every navigable canal and river staircase ever built
entries.notes: Qiao Weiyue invented the pound lock on China's Grand Canal in 984, replacing flash locks that wrecked grain barges; mitred European doors followed centuries later.

entries.name: Grand Canal (Da Yunhe)
entries.era: 5th c. BCE sections, joined by the Sui dynasty (581-618), still in use
entries.purpose: move grain and salt from the south to feed Beijing and the north
parts: lock flights on the Shandong rise
layout: three great reaches linked by ferry points and locks
summit level ~42 m above sea level in Shandong
barges tracked or towed by animal or human power
entries.found: across eastern China; the world's longest canal, still navigated
entries.notes: Older than any surviving European canal by a millennium; joining north and south culturally as much as economically.

entries.name: Pontoon (bridge of boats)
entries.purpose: cross a river fast, with no foundations, then strike it again
layout: floats spaced 3-6 m apart, deck lashed or hinged over them
held against the current by upstream moorings or heavy anchors
military bridges assemble from standard bays in hours
entries.found: at armies on the move and at emergency flood repairs
entries.notes: Herodotus records Darius bridging the Hellespont with about 600 ships in 512 BCE; when storms smashed it he had the sea whipped 300 times.

entries.name: Bascule (lift) bridge
entries.purpose: let road traffic cross while admitting tall ships through the navigation channel
parts: two fixed approach spans and towers
counterweight pits at the tower bases
layout: leaves pivot low, near the waterline; the heavy rear swings down as the front lifts
still and moving together: both leaves rise or both stay down
lifting sequence interlocked with river traffic signals
entries.found: where sea trade meets dense urban road traffic — old port cities
entries.notes: Tower Bridge (London, 1894) raises its bascules in about 5 minutes; steam-driven at opening, fully electric-hydraulic since 1976.

entries.name: Tidal causeway
entries.purpose: walk or drive to a tidal island twice a day, when the sea allows
parts: stone-cobbled track on a compacted fill
refuge huts on stilts for the caught
marker poles for the line of the road underwater
layout: dead-straight or gently curved track along the last exposed ridge of the seabed
passable only in the tide window; timetables published; warnings posted
causeway ends at a landing below the island's high-water mark
entries.found: to tidal islands and headlands — Holy Island (Lindisfarne), St Michael's Mount
entries.notes: Lindisfarne's pilgrim path has been crossed by monks for 1,300 years; misjudge the tide and it drowns twice daily.

entries.name: Lighthouse
entries.purpose: warning and position-fix for coastal shipping; mark harbor entrances and rocks
layout: tall round taper tower, unwindowed on the seaward side in hard weather
built on the outermost rock or head so it is seen against dark sky or land
characteristic flash pattern identifies the light to mariners
entries.found: on capes, reefs and harbor mouths wherever trade hugged a coast
entries.notes: The Pharos of Alexandria (c. 280 BCE) was a Wonder of the World; the Roman Tower of Hercules at A Coruña (2nd c. CE) still shines today.

entries.name: Breakwater / mole
entries.purpose: kill the swell so ships can moor and cargo can load in calm water
parts: long stone arm from the shore or a detached seawall
lighthouse or beacon at the head (often)
layout: arms curve to wrap the anchorage; often two arms leave a narrow gap as the entrance
crest just above storm wave height; core of graded rubble under armor
inside the mole the water is effectively a harbor even on an open coast
entries.found: on exposed coasts that became ports — Carthage, Portus near Rome, modern container ports
entries.notes: Claudius built Portus (46 CE) by sinking ship-timber caissons of hydraulic concrete in open sea — the largest marine concrete works of antiquity.

entries.name: Quay / quayside
entries.purpose: let ships moor against deep water so cargo can move straight between hold and wagon
layout: face set parallel to the berth line, depth at the wall enough for the largest expected ship
bollards every 10-20 m
open storage and transit sheds directly behind the face
entries.found: inside every working harbor; the quay, not the anchorage, is the harbor
entries.notes: The Phoenician and Roman ports of Byblos, Carthage and Portus all turned on quay walls; the principle has not changed in 3,000 years.

entries.name: Open-piled pier
entries.purpose: reach deep water past the surf zone without dredging to a quay
parts: piled bents out through the surf line
pavilions and landing at the seaward end
layout: deck elevated so waves pass under between bents
single narrow stem off the beach, widening into a landing head
often doubled as a promenade for the town behind it
entries.found: at gently shelving seaside resorts — the Victorian British coast above all
entries.notes: Brighton's Palace Pier (1899) mixed steamer berth with music-hall pavilion; hundreds of British piers rose 1850-1914.

entries.name: Dockside warehouse
entries.purpose: dry bulk storage at the berth; customs control of goods in bond
parts: raised floor above flood level on blocks or arches
layout: sited at the wharf head so cargo moves hold -> scale -> warehouse in one straight line
floor on piers or open arches to keep grain dry and walked by air
loading doors aligned to the quay edge
entries.found: at every port that handled grain — Lothal, Alexandria, Ostia, Amsterdam
entries.notes: Lothal's warehouse (c. 2400 BCE) stood on 64 fired-brick blocks with ~1.2 m ventilation passages — inventory and quality control 4,500 years ago.

entries.name: Covered market (bazaar / suq)
entries.purpose: all-weather retail heart of a trade city — the legal marketplace under one roof
parts: vaulted streets crossing at domed bays
layout: a grid or radial mesh of straight vaulted lanes by trade: goldsmiths, spice, textiles, leather
domes mark the junctions and the most prestigious pitches
shops a single structural bay wide — max ~5 m frontage
entries.found: at the meeting point of caravan roads inside old city walls
entries.notes: Istanbul's Grand Bazaar (founded c. 1461) still trades under ~61 covered streets and some 4,000 shops; one of the oldest roofed markets on Earth.

entries.name: Caravanserai
entries.era: 11th c. to 19th c. (some still host travelers)
entries.purpose: walled overnight hostel for caravans — merchants, pack animals and goods under one lock
parts: massive square outer wall, one defended gate
stables and stalls on the ground floor
layout: single defended gateway facing the road
courtyard with fountain/well; stalls along the inside wall
cells open off a covered gallery; roof flat for drying goods
entries.found: every ~30-40 km along Silk Road and hajj routes — a day's march apart
entries.notes: Anatolia bristles with them; Sultanhanı (1236) is the largest Seljuk example. They were the internet of their day: rumor, credit and news moved with the caravans.

entries.name: Turnpike toll gate
entries.purpose: collect road tolls to fund maintenance of a turnpike road
parts: pivoted boom arm across the road
layout: gate closes the full width of the road between the posts
booth adjacent to the driver's window for hand-to-hand payment
extra gates for riders and drovers; exemption for clergy and funerals (customary)
blueprint: layer 1: p a a a a p
legend: p stone post, a timber boom arm, . road/air
entries.found: on every toll road in 18th-19th century Britain and its colonies
entries.notes: The Rebecca Riots (1839-43) saw Welsh farming communities dismantle tollgates by night, dressed as women, in protest at the toll burden.

entries.name: Road milestone
entries.purpose: state the distance to the next city along a road
layout: set at the road edge, facing the oncoming traveller
one every Roman mile (1,480 m) on a Roman road; every mile or km since
inscription gives the emperor's titles and miles to the next caput viae
entries.found: lining the roads of every organized empire — Rome, Inca, Qing, British Raj
entries.notes: Roman milestones were recarved like tree rings as emperors came and went; surviving Via Appia stones still carry their distances.

entries.name: Horse-post relay station
entries.purpose: swap exhausted horses for fresh ones so an imperial dispatch never rides one animal to death
layout: built exactly a horse's hard gallop apart — 25 to 40 km
small, hard, minimal comfort; a post, not an inn
couriers carry a sealed badge; fodder and remounts prepaid by the state
entries.found: strung like beads along the Persian Royal Road, Roman cursus publicus and Mongol yam
entries.notes: Herodotus praised the Persian angareion — 'neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night stays these couriers' — still carved on the New York Post Office.

entries.name: Cable (reaction) ferry
materials: steel or wire-rope cable across the river
entries.purpose: cross a river using the current itself — no engine, no bridge
parts: fixed cable strung bank to bank at deck height
angled ferry hull with rudder rigged to the current
layout: ferry tethered to the cable; rudder set at a bias so the current pushes it diagonally downstream
boat sweeps a slow zigzag back and forth across the reach
works only on rivers with real current; replaced elsewhere by paddle or diesel ferries
entries.found: on tidal and swift rivers — the Scottish Connel Ferry tradition and the US Pacific coast
entries.notes: A reaction ferry is its own current-driven engine: free energy from the river, forever, as long as the cable holds.

entries.name: Funicular railway
entries.purpose: carry passengers straight up a slope too steep for a normal railway
parts: two cars on a single rope over a crown pulley
layout: two cars permanently coupled by the rope; one climbs as the other descends
single track with a staggered passing loop at the middle
cars counterbalance each other — the engine only fights friction
entries.found: on steep city hills and resort slopes — Lyon, Montmartre, Valparaíso
entries.notes: Fourvière (Lyon, 1862) and Montmartre (Paris, 1900) prototypes still climb; a funicular sips a fraction of the energy of a rack railway.

entries.name: Aerial material ropeway
entries.purpose: haul ore, limestone or timber over terrain no road or rail can cross
parts: endless loop of rope over tower-sheave lines
buckets detached at load and dump stations
tensioning weights at the tail station
layout: straight line of towers from mine/quarry to tip or railhead
downhill loaded, uphill empty — gravity does half the work
towers scaled to keep buckets clear of the ground and hillside
entries.found: above Alpine mines and quarries; many still run a century after installation
entries.notes: Adolf Bleichert's firm built ropeways from 1874; they hauled 10-100+ tonnes an hour on lines roads never reached.

entries.name: Container terminal
entries.purpose: transfer intermodal TEU/FEU containers between ship, rail and truck
layout: cranes on rails parallel to the berth; yard blocks behind in strict rows
traffic segregated: quay cranes -> yard -> gate with no crossings
modern terminals automated — driverless shuttles, camera OCR at the gates
entries.found: at every deep-water anchorage in world trade — Rotterdam, Singapore, Shanghai
entries.notes: Malcom McLean's Ideal X carried 58 containers Newark-Houston in April 1956; the box cut port labor and time so hard it redrew global trade.

entries.name: Lothal tidal dockyard
entries.purpose: tidal berthing and repair yard for a seagoing trade city
parts: rectangular dock basin with vertical fired-brick walls
inlet and outlet channels with sluice pens
warehouse on 64 brick piers at the wharf head
layout: basin oriented along the river; ships enter on the tide through the northern inlet
sluice gates held water in against the falling tide for berthing at low water
warehouse directly behind the wharf for sealed customs control
entries.found: at Lothal, on the Bhogava river near the Gulf of Khambhat, Gujarat, India
entries.notes: Among the world's oldest known dockyards — contemporary with the Great Pyramid; its tidal sluice logic matches modern lock practice.

entries.name: Aqueduct bridge
materials: dressed limestone (no mortar at Pont du Gard)
entries.purpose: gravity delivery of water across a valley — bulk transport of water, not people
layout: constant gentle gradient (~1:3000) from mountain spring to city castellum
three tiers of arches at the high point; single tier or arcade elsewhere
channel roofed with slabs against contamination
entries.found: where a city needed river-fed water and could build stone in volume — Nîmes, Segovia, Constantinople
entries.notes: Pont du Gard (Gardon valley, c. 40-60 CE, 275 m long, 49 m high) carried ~20,000 m³ of water a day to Nîmes; today a UNESCO site.

entries.name: Mountain pass (col)
entries.purpose: the lowest line through a ridge — the natural corridor every road and railway of that range still uses
parts: often a hospice or toll station (human overlay)
layout: single line through the ridge where the crest dips lowest
flanked by cliffs; weather and snow decide the season of use
road, pack train, or railway tunnel follows the same geological weakness
entries.found: wherever a range pinches low — Khyber, Gotthard, Brenner, St Bernard
entries.notes: The Khyber Pass (~1,070 m) threaded the trade roads between Central and South Asia for 2,000 years; armies and goods both had to funnel through it.

entries.name: River ford
entries.purpose: the shallowest wadeable point of a river — every bridge on that river was built here first
parts: firm shallow bar of gravel or rock
old track alignment on both sides
layout: where the river spreads wide and shallow over a resistant bar
track approaches perpendicular to flow, marked by worn ruts
bridge site, mill site and town site all inherited from the ford
entries.found: upstream of bridge sites; fossilized in place-names like Oxford and Stratford
entries.notes: Oxford is literally the oxen's ford. The Romans bridged many rivers exactly where centuries of traffic had already picked the crossing.

entries.name: Natural harbour
materials: drowned river valley (ria) or glacial trough (fjord) scenery
entries.purpose: free sheltered anchorage for a fleet — the single biggest head-start geography can give a port
parts: fresh water and gently shelving landing points
layout: wide deep basin behind a narrow mouth; forbids the open-sea swell
multiple river deltas or creeks giving wharf-able frontage
settlement clusters at the head of the harbour where goods land
entries.found: on every coast that became a trade power — Sydney, Hong Kong, Pearl Harbor, Fiume
entries.notes: Sydney (Port Jackson, First Fleet 1788) needed zero breakwater; natural harbours pre-built by drowned valleys are why some cities became ports and others never did.
